source_read: PMC HTML (PMC3479587; the published PNAS version, not an author manuscript), full text read on 2026-10-27: Abstract, introduction, Results with Tables 1-5 (read from the HTML text), Discussion, Methods, and the Author Summary (PNAS 109(40):15980) printed with it. Fig. 2 and Fig. 3 read on screen and from enlarged screenshots (values approximate); Fig. 1 not inspected (its content taken from the Results text). Online supplement (Tables S1-S3, Fig. S1) not read. Written up on 2026-10-30 from the saved text after the browser became unreachable.

claims.overstatement: None as to strength: the claim rightly says this is not a test of abstinence. The exposure is misdefined (see note).
claims.note: Numbers check against Fig. 3: 17 people, p = .03, use weekly or less in the year before the age-38 test, median 14 days (range 0-52), childhood about 102 to adult about 97.5 (my reading 102.2 to 97.5). Error in the exposure: Fig. 3 is restricted to people with dependence at 2 or more of the five interviews and splits them by onset of at least weekly cannabis use before 18 (panel label: used cannabis weekly before age 18), not by onset of dependence before 18. 'Persistent dependence that began in adolescence' (statement) and 'adolescent-onset persistent dependence' (magnitude) should read, for example, 'people with dependence at two or more interviews who had used cannabis weekly before 18'. The paper does not say what test gives p = .03 (a within-group childhood-to-adult comparison). There is no never-user comparison in this analysis. Frequent adolescent-onset users (n = 19) fell more (about 96.8 to 89.2, p = .0002), and neither adult-onset group changed significantly (p = .73 and .11). The authors describe these people as having quit or reduced use for a year or more (Discussion, 2nd and 4th paragraphs), which goes beyond the figure's definition (up to 52 days of use in that year, self-reported); the claim's 'not a test of abstinence' is the right reading. The Fig. 3 groups total 69, against 73 people with 2 or more waves of dependence in Table 1, with no explanation given.

anchors.locator: Results › What Is the Effect of Cessation of Cannabis Use?, 1st paragraph; Fig. 3 (caption and panel labels)
anchors.extracted: Restricted to persistent users, defined as dependence at 2 or more waves; grouped by onset of at least weekly cannabis use before 18 and by use in the year before the age-38 test (infrequent = weekly or less: adolescent-onset median 14 days, range 0-52; adult-onset median 6, range 0-52; frequent: median 365, range 100-365). Childhood against age-38 full-scale IQ within each group, values read from the figure: adolescent-onset infrequent n = 17, about 102.2 to 97.5, p = .03; adolescent-onset frequent n = 19, about 96.8 to 89.2, p = .0002; adult-onset infrequent n = 13, about 104.4 to 105.4, p = .73; adult-onset frequent n = 20, about 98.6 to 95.7, p = .11. No never-user group in this analysis; test not described; error bars are SEs.

anchors.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph (fifth point) and 4th paragraph (second and fourth limitations); Abstract
anchors.extracted: Authors conclude that in adolescent-onset former persistent users impairment remained after cessation for a year or more and that cessation did not fully restore functioning (Abstract), while calling reversibility a question for further research. The 'cessation' group as defined in Fig. 3 includes people who used up to weekly (0-52 days) in the year before testing; use was self-reported with no biological verification (Discussion, 4th paragraph).

claims.overstatement: Slight: calling all 16 'memory, speed and executive tests' makes the result look broader within those domains than it is (7 of 14), and the 16 tests were not corrected for multiple comparisons. The claim's closing caution (no comparison can show causation) fits this source.
claims.note: Exposure (number of the five interviews from 18 to 38 at which dependence criteria were met, as a five-level score whose lowest two levels separate never-users from people who used but were never dependent), adjustment (childhood full-scale IQ and sex) and 'not given in childhood' all match. The count 9 of 16 matches Table 3, but the 16 scores are 5 executive, 6 memory, 3 processing-speed, 1 perceptual-reasoning and 1 verbal-comprehension score; 2 of the 9 significant ones are the WAIS-IV Perceptual Reasoning and Verbal Comprehension indexes, so the memory, speed and executive tests alone give 7 of 14. Suggested wording: '9 of 16 tests of memory, speed, executive function, reasoning and verbal comprehension'. All 9 go in the direction of poorer scores; none of the 5 time or error scores (higher = worse) was significant. No correction for multiple testing is reported (editors' calculation: at 0.05/16 = 0.003, 3 of 16 remain: Months of the Year Backward, Processing Speed Index, Verbal Comprehension Index). The authors' test that the four WAIS-IV index associations could be set equal (chi-square change 2.13, df = 3, P = 0.55) means no domain stood out.

anchors.locator: Results › Is Impairment Specific to Certain Neuropsychological Domains or Is It Global?, 1st paragraph; Table 3 and its footnote
anchors.extracted: Age-38 tests: 16 scores (executive 5, memory 6, processing speed 3, perceptual reasoning 1, verbal comprehension 1) as standardized means adjusted for childhood full-scale IQ; OLS linear trend over the five dependence-persistence groups controlling for childhood IQ and sex. P < .05 for 9: WAIS-IV Working Memory Index t = −2.16, Months of the Year Backward −5.24, RVIP A prime −2.58, Rey total recall −2.65, Rey delayed recall −2.11, Paired Associates Learning first-trial memory −2.22, WAIS-IV Processing Speed Index −3.64, Perceptual Reasoning Index −2.33, Verbal Comprehension Index −3.04. Not significant: Trail-Making B, RVIP false alarms, Verbal Paired Associates total and delayed, PAL total errors, RVIP mean latency, 5-choice reaction time. 3+ group, e.g., Processing Speed −0.61, Months Backward −0.63, Rey total −0.48 (never-users 0.14, 0.24, 0.11). Setting the four WAIS-IV index associations equal did not worsen fit (chi-square change 2.13, df = 3, P = 0.55). No multiple-testing correction reported.

Tests given only in adulthood were analysed by OLS regression with childhood full-scale IQ as a covariate (residualized change); persistence entered as a five-level score (1 to 5); sex a covariate in all tests; tables give the t test for the linear effect.

claims.overstatement: None from this source: the claim keeps to association, reports the fall in the test statistic under fuller adjustment and attributes the 8 points to 23 people. One misstatement: 'with no test of the difference' (Fig. 2 prints p = .02).
claims.note: All Meier 2012 numbers check: 874 = 242 + 479 + 80 + 35 + 38; 38/874 = 4.3% (about 4 in 100); 81.58% male; 99.84 to 100.64 (+0.05 SD) and 99.68 to 93.93 (5.75 points, −0.38 SD; about 6, as the text says); t = −4.45 (sex-adjusted), −3.41 (education), −2.20 (multivariable; −2.20/−4.45 = 0.49, so 'about halved' holds); 7 cohort members had tried cannabis by 13; Fig. 2 read as −0.54 (n = 23) and −0.14 (n = 14). Corrections: (1) 'with no test of the difference' is contradicted by Fig. 2, which gives p = .02 for adolescent- against adult-onset dependence at 3 or more waves (p = .44 at 1 wave, .09 at 2); the paper does not say what test this is and reports no interaction test, so the statement could say 'p = .02 by a test the paper does not describe; not significant at 1 or 2 waves'. The magnitude already gives p = .02, so statement and magnitude disagree. (2) In the multivariable model 'recent use' is past-24-hour use only; past-week use was handled only by exclusion. (3) The magnitude labels the group change scores 'sex-adjusted', but each equals the raw mean change divided by 15 (Table 1), so they are unadjusted; only the trend tests are sex-adjusted. Not in the claim and worth knowing: the trend held without the 3+ group (t = −2.94); persistent regular use (4 or more days a week) gave a similar gradient (3+ waves, n = 41: 96.00 to 90.77, −0.35); the Fig. 2 groups (74, 33, 37) fall short of Table 1's (80, 35, 38) without explanation; no coefficient, standard error or interval is reported for any trend; the authors say causality cannot be established and that adjusting for education may be overcontrol.

anchors.extracted: Dunedin Study: complete birth cohort of consecutive births in Dunedin, New Zealand, 1 April 1972 to 31 March 1973; 1,037 children (91% of eligible births; 52% boys); assessed at 38 in 2010-2012, when 96% of the 1,004 living members took part.

anchors.locator: Methods › Measures › Neuropsychological functioning, 1st paragraph; Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: IQ tested at 7, 9, 11 and 13 (WISC-R) before cannabis use began (only 7 members had tried cannabis by 13) and at 38 (WAIS-IV), both mean 100, SD 15. Childhood IQ = mean of ages 7-13 (7-11 for the 7 who had tried cannabis by 13); change = adult minus childhood IQ; OLS trend over a five-level persistence score; sex a covariate in all tests.

anchors.locator: Methods › Measures › Cannabis use, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Past-year DSM cannabis dependence by Diagnostic Interview Schedule at 18, 21, 26, 32 and 38; exposure = number of the five waves with dependence (never used; used, never dependent; 1; 2; 3 or more); members missing 3 or more of the 5 waves excluded (97% of living members included). Alternative exposure: waves with use on 4 or more days a week (weighted kappa with the dependence grouping 0.77).

anchors.locator: Table 1 (persistence of cannabis dependence rows); Results › Do Study Members with More Persistent Cannabis Use Show Greater IQ Decline?, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: n = 242 never used, 479 used but never dependent, 80 dependent at 1 wave, 35 at 2, 38 at 3 or more (total 874); % male 38.84, 49.48, 70.00, 62.86, 81.58. Childhood to age-38 full-scale IQ: never used 99.84 (SD 14.39) to 100.64 (15.25), change +0.05 SD; 3 or more waves 99.68 (13.53) to 93.93 (13.32), change −0.38 SD, about 6 points per the text; −0.07, −0.11 and −0.17 in the middle groups. Each change equals (adult minus child mean)/15 (e.g., 5.75/15 = 0.383), so the group values are unadjusted. Regular-use grouping similar (3 or more waves, n = 41: 96.00 to 90.77, −0.35).

anchors.locator: Table 2, full-scale IQ row and footnote
anchors.extracted: Linear trend over the five groups t = −4.45, P < 0.0001, OLS controlling for sex; Verbal IQ t = −4.15, Performance IQ t = −2.84; no coefficient, standard error or confidence interval reported.

anchors.locator: Results › Do Study Members with More Persistent Cannabis Use Show Greater IQ Decline?, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Trend in full-scale IQ change still present after excluding the 3+ group: t = −2.94, P = 0.0034.

anchors.locator: Results › Is Impairment Attributable to Persistent Cannabis Use or Are There Alternative Explanations?, 1st paragraph; Fig. 1 caption
anchors.extracted: Excluding, one group at a time, people who used cannabis in the past 24 h or the past week (asked on the test day at 38), people with tobacco, hard-drug or alcohol dependence at 3 or more waves, and people with lifetime schizophrenia left the effect sizes for full-scale IQ change virtually the same and significant (figure values not read; subtests in supplementary Table S2, not read). Multivariable model adjusting together for past-24-h cannabis use, number of waves of tobacco, hard-drug and alcohol dependence, and schizophrenia: t = −2.20, P = 0.0282 (about half the sex-only t of −4.45).

anchors.locator: Results › Is Impairment Apparent Even After Controlling for Years of Education?, 1st paragraph; Table 4
anchors.extracted: Trend t = −3.41, P = 0.0007 after adjusting for years of education (−4.45 before); fewer persistent users had education beyond high school (chi-square 63.94, P < 0.0001); among members with high-school education or less, change −0.03 (n = 59), −0.14 (130), −0.16 (43), −0.25 (20), −0.48 (26), trend t = −3.36, P = 0.0009.

anchors.locator: Results › Are Adolescent Cannabis Users Particularly Vulnerable?, 1st paragraph; Fig. 2 (bars and caption)
anchors.extracted: Onset of dependence before 18 against not dependent before 18, within each persistence level (values read from the figure, SD units): 1 wave about −0.22 (n = 17) against −0.08 (n = 57); 2 waves about −0.39 (12) against −0.03 (21); 3 or more about −0.54 (23) against −0.14 (14). Caption: about −0.55 SD in the adolescent-onset 3+ group = 8 IQ points. Text: adult-onset users showed no decline with persistence; a weekly-use-before-18 definition gave similar results (Fig. S1, supplement, not read; kappa 0.64 between definitions). Figure group sizes (74, 33, 37) are smaller than Table 1's (80, 35, 38), unexplained.

anchors.locator: Fig. 2 (p-value brackets under each pair of bars)
anchors.extracted: Adolescent- against adult-onset compared within each level: p = .44 (1 wave), p = .09 (2 waves), p = .02 (3 or more waves); test not described in the text or Methods; no interaction test reported. Contradicts 'with no test of the difference'.

The 8-point decline is that of the most persistent adolescent-onset users (n = 23, Author Summary). The Author Summary also gives 5-6 points for the most persistent regular users (n = 41; Table P1: 96.00 to 90.77).

Authors state the data cannot definitively show that the association is causal and an unknown third variable could explain it; they argue that adjusting for education may be overcontrol if cannabis lowers schooling.
Cannabis use and dependence were self-reported past-year measures with no biological validation; findings come from one cohort born in Dunedin in the 1970s.

key_findings.note: The five assessment ages for dependence and frequency are in Methods › Measures › Cannabis use, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; the locator could add that subsection.

All values match Table 1. Each group change equals the raw adult-minus-child mean divided by 15 (e.g., 5.75/15 = 0.383), so the group values are unadjusted and only the trend tests are sex-adjusted; worth saying, because one claim's magnitude labels the group values sex-adjusted.
Table 2 and the 2nd paragraph match (Information t = −2.40, Similarities −2.78, Vocabulary −3.67, Digit Symbol −5.60).

Of the 9 significant scores, 2 are the WAIS-IV Perceptual Reasoning (t = −2.33) and Verbal Comprehension (t = −3.04) indexes, so the memory, speed and executive tests alone give 7 of 14. The three other non-significant measures are RVIP false alarms (P = 0.96), PAL total errors (0.16) and RVIP mean latency (0.06).

key_findings.correction: Not an error found in the card; part of this finding could not be checked. The text part is confirmed: excluding each group in turn left the IQ-change estimates virtually the same and significant, and the multivariable model with past-24-hour use, number of waves of tobacco, hard-drug and alcohol dependence, and schizophrenia gave t = −2.20, P = 0.0282 (Results › Is Impairment Attributable…, 1st paragraph). The excluded-group sizes (38, 89, 126, 7, 53, 28) and the full-cohort n = 874 are printed only in the Fig. 1 key, which I did not inspect before the browser became unreachable; they need a targeted check, as do the same n values repeated in the card's sample, exposure and polysubstance fields.

key_findings.note: Table 5 n values sum to 822. The memory-problems mean is slightly higher at 2 waves (0.78) than at 3 or more (0.75).

My readings from an enlarged screenshot: −0.22 against −0.08, −0.39 against −0.03, −0.54 against −0.14; n and p values as printed (17/57, 12/21, 23/14; .44, .09, .02). Weighted means of the strata reproduce Table 1 (e.g., 3+: (23 × −0.54 + 14 × −0.14)/37 = −0.39).
My readings: 102.2 to 97.5; 96.8 to 89.2; 104.4 to 105.4; 98.6 to 95.7. The panel labels confirm that onset here is weekly use before 18 (used / did not use cannabis weekly before age 18).

reporting_issues.note: Abstract: testing at 13 and 38; Methods: IQ averaged over 7-13, other tests only at 38.
This is the distinction that the after-stopping claim misses (it describes the Fig. 3 group as dependence beginning in adolescence).

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E, high overall, driven by confounding: the main models adjust for sex only, and no SES, family or personality covariate enters this paper. The other domain judgments fit what I read. The Fig. 1 n values cited in the missing-data and exposure notes were not checked by me (see key finding 5).

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: 'cessation for a year or more', 'global' decline, 'ruled out premorbid deficit' and the 8-point figure go beyond the tabulated results, as the card sets out.

missed: The test behind the p values printed on Figs. 2 and 3 (the onset contrasts within each persistence level and the child-against-adult comparisons) is not described in the Methods, so it is not known how they were computed or whether they are sex-adjusted like the trend tests. Key finding 8 could also say in so many words that p = .02 is a printed between-onset test at 3 or more waves, since one claim states that no such test was made.
